clinicalPearls: The commonest germ cell tumour of the anterior mediastinum, usually a mature (benign) lesion containing tissues from more than one germ layer
Sits within the classic anterior-mediastinal 'four Ts' differential alongside thymoma, thyroid masses, and 'terrible' lymphoma
Often asymptomatic and found incidentally, but may cause chest pain, cough, or breathlessness through mass effect
Cross-sectional imaging typically shows a heterogeneous mass containing fat, fluid, soft tissue, and calcification, sometimes with a recognisable tooth
Coughing up hair or sebaceous material (trichoptysis) is a rare but essentially diagnostic feature when a teratoma erodes into an airway
Mature teratomas are benign, whereas immature or malignant germ cell elements alter management and prognosis
Complete surgical resection is both diagnostic and curative for mature lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Mediastinal teratomas are thought to arise from primordial germ cells that fail to complete their migration and become mislocated within the mediastinum during embryogenesis. These pluripotent cells give rise to tissues derived from all three germ layers, so the resulting mass typically contains a mixture of ectodermal skin and hair, mesodermal fat and cartilage, and endodermal glandular elements, accounting for the characteristic heterogeneous imaging appearance with fat and calcification. Mature teratomas are well differentiated and benign, but tumours containing immature tissue or other malignant germ cell components behave more aggressively and may secrete tumour markers.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant mediastinal germ cell tumour (seminomatous or non-seminomatous)
Thymic cyst or other foregut cyst
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax showing fat, fluid, and calcific components
MRI to further characterise tissue components and delineate adjacent structures
Serum alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin to help exclude malignant germ cell elements
Biopsy in selected cases where imaging is indeterminate or malignancy is suspected
PET-CT where a malignant or immature component is a concern
redFlags: Raised alpha-fetoprotein or beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin suggesting a malignant germ cell component
Rapid growth or invasion of adjacent structures on imaging
Superior vena caval obstruction or airway compromise from mass effect
Trichoptysis or rupture into an airway, pleura, or pericardium
reference.prognosis: Completely resected mature teratomas have an excellent prognosis and are effectively cured, whereas immature or malignant germ cell tumours require multimodality treatment and carry a more guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming any anterior mediastinal mass is a thymoma without considering a teratoma
Failing to measure germ cell tumour markers before treatment planning
Mistaking a malignant germ cell tumour for a benign teratoma on limited sampling
Underestimating the technical difficulty of resecting a mass densely adherent to great vessels
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Complete surgical resection as the definitive, curative treatment for mature (benign) teratoma
Measure alpha-fetoprotein and beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin to detect malignant germ-cell elements that change management
Cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by resection of residual disease where immature or malignant components are present
Manage local mass effect on the airway, great vessels and oesophagus, including erosion into an airway causing trichoptysis
Post-resection surveillance imaging to detect recurrence, particularly with immature or malignant elements
Coordinate care through a thoracic surgery and oncology multidisciplinary team
